Slatwall · Prusa MK4 · PETG

Slatwall Bracket Study

How light can a 3D-printed shelf bracket get and still hold a loaded 200 mm shelf for years? Nine designs, from Maillart and Gaudí to pure optimization, all sized for the same job and checked with the same physics.

46 gbest bracket (Hanging arch + rest)
13.9 kgsafe load, per bracket
0.30kg held per gram
The job

One bracket, one shelf, one printer

  • Shelf: 200 mm deep, load spread along the top or all on the front edge. Two brackets per shelf; numbers below are per bracket.
  • Wall: slatwall verified to fit ProSlat carbon fiber panels, slots 10 mm open at a measured 4 3/4" (120.65 mm) pitch. Every bracket uses our fit-tested hook in the upper slot; most also rest a tab in the next slot down.
  • Printer: MK4 with the 0.6 HF nozzle. The bracket prints flat, so it has to fit the 250 × 210 mm bed: about 215 × 150 mm, two slots tall at most.
  • "Safe": the smallest of three limits. Creep: stress under 10 MPa so it doesn't sag over months. Strength: half of PETG's tensile strength. Buckling: a factor of 3 on the load where a strut bows out.

What the physics says

Findings

Height beats everything

The hook gets pulled out with roughly load × depth ÷ bracket height. A bracket one slot tall pulls the hook 2.5× harder than one reaching toward the next slot, so every good design uses the full two-slot height.

Buckling, not breaking

PETG is soft (about 1.6 GPa). Long thin struts bow sideways long before the plastic tears. Most designs end up limited by buckling or by creep, almost never by strength.

The wall only pushes

A frictionless wall can't hold anything up, which forced the optimizer into hanging ties. Resting a tab in the next slot down gives a second support that carries weight, and makes even two bars competitive.

Build members from perimeters

Thin members are sized to an exact number of perimeters (1.17, 1.74 or 2.30 mm), so they print as continuous loops with no infill: the strongest thing a printer makes.

Twin walls for compression

Two perimeter walls held apart by zig-zag lacing, like a crane boom, resist bowing far better per gram than a solid strut. That ladder arch is what puts the hanging arch on top.

Thickness is free

The part prints flat, so the hook region can be printed taller than the truss at no cost. The hook is the most stressed spot on every design.

Catalog

The designs

Each design was sized by an automated search: least plastic that still holds about 15 kg (some land a bit under after correcting PETG's stiffness). Every candidate was checked with the full simulation.

Your two suggestions applied to the hanging arch: the arch foot now sits in the next slot down, and a spine along the wall was offered to the search. The rest tab helps (about 7% better). How we got here

From a blob to a truss

Materials

Same shapes, other filaments

A design's stress pattern doesn't depend on the material, so each design can be re-scored from its PETG simulation: buckling scales with stiffness, creep and strength with each material's allowables, and weight with density. Shapes stay as sized for PETG; a stiffer material would let them get thinner still.

Fine print

Method and limits

  • Simulation: 2D plane-stress finite elements on a 0.4 mm grid of the printed profile. The bracket prints flat, so every in-plane load runs along the layers. Wall contact is one-sided: the hook bears on the slot floor and lip, the bracket pushes on the wall face, the rest tab sits on the lower slot floor.
  • Buckling: linear eigenvalue analysis of the actual geometry (solid material only), safety factor 3.
  • Checked against beam theory (tip deflection within 0.3%). The rest tab and hook were checked for tilt-in insertion with a separate motion simulator.
  • Not modelled: twisting out of the bracket's plane (the shelf deck tying two brackets together handles that), stress at sharp joints (small fillets are added), print defects, and temperature. Treat absolute numbers as ±20% until a load test; the ranking is the reliable part.
  • Material: Prusament PETG, 1.6 GPa, 0.15 mm layers. Sizing searches ran at 2.0 GPa and all final numbers were re-checked at 1.6.
Next

What to print

  • Print the leading design and the two-bar minimalist in PETG and load-test both with water jugs on a short shelf: add 2 kg at a time, and note the deflection at the tip and anything that creaks.
  • If you want more margin without more weight, print the same file in PC-CF or annealed PET-CF.
  • Print-ready: bracket/out/print/hanging_arch_rest.3mf (0.40 mm STRUCTURAL, PETG, 3 perimeters, 100% infill, about 1 h 22 m, 45 g). Re-sized for 0.40 mm perimeters and given a thin wall spine: 14.4 kg safe per bracket.
  • Everything lives in bracket/ of the slatwall-accessories repo: the solver, every design, and STLs for all of them.
